newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Mir crew relaxes, major repairs delayed.
newsitem.headline: Russian Mir crew relaxes, major repairs delayed.

text.p: The crew of Russia's damaged Mir space station, who regained control after a self-inflicted crisis, were given a day of rest on Saturday, while officials discussed their next steps.
An official from the U.S. space agency NASA said Russians Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin and American Michael Foale would only do some minor repairs during the day.

"They will be spending most of the time resting except they are working on two gyrodynes," Kathleen Maliga told reporters at the Mission Control outside Moscow, referring to devices that keep Mir's solar panels lined up on the Sun.

The station's 12 gyrodynes stopped working and the crippled space station briefly lost its orientation when one of the crew -- officials will not say who -- pulled out a cable and crashed a vital computer on Thursday.

Maliga said the crew restarted seven gyrodynes on Friday and were working on two more on Saturday. For some time after the computer crash the the panels were being held in alignment by electronically controlled motors.
Mission director Vladimir Solovyov told a news briefing that the station's orientation was now being maintained again by the energy-saving gyrodynes but added that they needed extra checks.

The computer mishap has added to the latest string of misfortunes haunting the crew of the ageing space laboratory, which began when a Progress cargo craft holed the Spektr scientific module on June 25 during a practice docking.
The incident, which deprived the station of nearly half its energy resources, was followed by a mysterious leak of unidentified liquid and heart problems suffered by mission commander Tsibliyev.
Experts on earth, who have held consultations after the latest incident, appear to have decided that the main repairs on board will be carried out by the next crew due to reach Mir on August 7.
Two fresh Russian cosmonauts, Pavel Vinogradov and Anatoly Solovyov, are already in training at Star City near Moscow for the dangerous job of entering the airless Spektr module.
"The intensive training in Star City showed that some special instruments will be needed to make the repairs safe for the cosmonauts," Solovyov said.
"These instruments can only be delivered by the next space craft and then it will be highly unreasonable to send the weary old crew to do the repairs rather then the fresh new crew," he added.
But the final decision on the future plans, Solovyov said, would be taken by a meeting of senior officials at Mission Control planned for Monday.
He said the cosmonauts took things calmly but were not too happy to hear the news.
"They realise it was a reasonable decision but they were certainly upset," he said adding that Mission Control tried to calm the crew's possible worries.
"We told the crew that they did a great job and that they should not blame themselves because of this accident," he said, pointing out the high level of stress to which the crew had been subjected.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin had planned to return to Earth on August 26, with British-born NASA physicist Foale going home as planned aboard a U.S. Shuttle in September.
Solovyov said the space mission of French cosmonaut Leopold Eyharts, which had been scheduled to blast off in the next Soyuz craft with the two Russians on August 5, was sure to be postponed.
"The huge cargo which needs to be taken to the Mir does not allow room for a third person in the Soyuz spacecraft," he said.
Solovyov said the modules where Eyharts was to conduct his experiments had lost power supply after the June 25 collision.
"I believe the French understand that there is no use going to space without a chance to carry out a scientific programme," he added. "We will repair the station and invite the French to come later."
